questions.stem: How many lattice points lie on the segment from (0,0) to (12,8), including both endpoints?

hint.level_0: The number of lattice points on a segment is controlled by the gcd of the coordinate differences — why?

questions.solution: Step 1 — Interior lattice points = gcd(12,8) − 1; gcd(12,8) = 4. Step 2 — Add the 2 endpoints: gcd+1. Step 3 — = 5.

questions.stem: How many diagonals does a convex 8-gon have?

hint.level_0: Each vertex connects to all others except itself and its two neighbours — then correct for double counting.

solution_steps: Each of 8 vertices has 8−3 diagonals; that counts each twice.
questions.solution: Step 1 — Each of 8 vertices has 8−3 diagonals; that counts each twice. Step 2 — n(n−3)/2 = 8·5/2. Step 3 — = 20.

questions.stem: In a convex 6-gon with no three diagonals concurrent, how many interior points are diagonal intersections?

hint.level_0: Each interior crossing is made by two diagonals, i.e. determined by how many of the polygon's vertices?

solution_steps: Two crossing diagonals use 4 distinct vertices, and any 4 vertices give exactly one crossing.
questions.solution: Step 1 — Two crossing diagonals use 4 distinct vertices, and any 4 vertices give exactly one crossing. Step 2 — So the count is C(6,4). Step 3 — = 15.

questions.stem: In how many ways can a convex 6-gon be cut into triangles by non-crossing diagonals (triangulations)?

hint.level_0: The number of triangulations of a convex polygon is a Catalan number — which index goes with an n-gon?

questions.solution: Step 1 — A convex (n)-gon has C_(n−2) triangulations. Step 2 — C_4 = Catalan(4). Step 3 — = 14.

questions.solution: Step 1 — Any 3 of the 7 points form a triangle (no 3 collinear). Step 2 — C(7,3). Step 3 — = 35.

questions.stem: Into how many regions do all the diagonals of a convex 5-gon (no three concurrent) divide its interior?

hint.level_0: Start from 1 region and add one each time a diagonal enters, plus one for every interior crossing (Euler's idea). How many crossings are there?

solution_steps: Regions = 1 + (diagonals) + (interior crossings), which simplifies to C(n,4)+C(n,2)−n+1.
questions.solution: Step 1 — Regions = 1 + (diagonals) + (interior crossings), which simplifies to C(n,4)+C(n,2)−n+1. Step 2 — = C(5,4)+C(5,2)−5+1. Step 3 — = 11.

questions.stem: What is the maximum number of regions the plane can be divided into by 5 straight lines?

hint.level_0: Each new line, if it crosses all previous ones, adds as many regions as the number of times it is cut, plus one. What's the running total?

solution_steps: The k-th line adds k regions; total = 1 + (1+2+…+5).
questions.solution: Step 1 — The k-th line adds k regions; total = 1 + (1+2+…+5). Step 2 — 1 + n(n+1)/2 = 1 + 5·6/2. Step 3 — = 16.

questions.stem: What is the maximum number of regions a circle's interior can be divided into by 4 chords (in general position)?

hint.level_0: Begin with 1 region; each chord adds 1, plus one extra for every interior crossing it makes. How many crossings can {n} chords have?

questions.solution: Step 1 — Regions = 1 + (chords) + (crossings) = 1 + 4 + C(4,2). Step 2 — = 1 + 4 + 6. Step 3 — = 11.

solution_steps: There are 4 vertical and 5 horizontal lines.

questions.stem: How many squares (of all sizes) are there in an 3×3 grid of unit cells?

hint.level_0: Count k×k squares separately for each side length k — how many positions does a k×k square have?

solution_steps: A k×k square fits in (3−k+1)² positions.
questions.solution: Step 1 — A k×k square fits in (3−k+1)² positions. Step 2 — Sum over k=1..3: Σ (3−k+1)². Step 3 — = 14.

questions.stem: There are 4 points on one line and 5 points on a parallel line. How many triangles have their vertices among these points?

hint.level_0: A triangle needs vertices not all on one line — so it takes 2 points from one line and 1 from the other. Count both ways.

solution_steps: Either 1 point from line A and 2 from line B, or 2 from A and 1 from B.
questions.solution: Step 1 — Either 1 point from line A and 2 from line B, or 2 from A and 1 from B. Step 2 — 4·C(5,2) + 5·C(4,2). Step 3 — = 70.

questions.solution: Step 1 — All triples: C(10,3) = 120. Step 2 — Degenerate (the 4 collinear): C(4,3) = 4. Step 3 — 120 − 4 = 116.

questions.stem: In how many ways can a 2×4 board be tiled by 1×2 dominoes?

hint.level_0: Consider the leftmost column: one vertical domino, or two horizontals stacked. What recurrence appears?

questions.solution: Step 1 — Vertical domino → 2×(4−1); two horizontals → 2×(4−2). Step 2 — T(n)=T(n−1)+T(n−2) (Fibonacci). Step 3 — T(4) = 5.

questions.stem: In how many ways can a 1×5 strip be tiled using tiles of length 1, 2 and 3?

hint.level_0: Look at the last tile (length 1, 2 or 3): each choice leaves a shorter strip. What three-term recurrence results?

questions.solution: Step 1 — f(n)=f(n−1)+f(n−2)+f(n−3) (tribonacci), f(0)=1,f(1)=1,f(2)=2. Step 2 — Build up to n=5. Step 3 — = 13.

questions.stem: How many distinct necklaces of 6 beads can be made with 2 colours, where rotations are considered the same?

hint.level_0: Average the colourings fixed by each rotation (Burnside). A rotation by d positions fixes colourings constant on its cycles — how many cycles?

solution_steps: Evaluate the sum over divisors d of 6.
questions.solution: Step 1 — Burnside over the 6 rotations: (1/6)·Σ_d φ(d)·2^(n/d). Step 2 — Evaluate the sum over divisors d of 6. Step 3 — = 14.

solution_steps: Evaluate the sum over divisors d of 5.

questions.stem: In how many distinct ways can the 6 faces of a cube be coloured with 2 colours, where rotations of the cube are considered the same?

hint.level_0: The cube's rotation group has 24 elements; average the colourings each rotation fixes (Burnside).

questions.solution: Step 1 — Burnside over the 24 rotations gives (k⁶+3k⁴+12k³+8k²)/24. Step 2 — Plug k=2. Step 3 — = 10.
